title: Keeping the Evening Tutoring Pilot
description: Locate evidence that directly supports a specific claim and distinguish it from background, limitations, and recommendations.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewNotes: Focused Arguments practice reviewed for one-best-answer logic, evidence fidelity, close distractors, and source-faithful explanations.

questions.prompt: Which detail provides the most direct evidence for Raman's claim that the tutoring program may help students academically?

options.text: The community center is served by an evening bus route.
options.whyWrong: The bus route supports the access argument, not the claim about academic improvement.

options.text: Several students stopped attending after sports seasons began.
options.whyWrong: This is a limitation of attendance, not evidence of academic benefit.

options.text: Of 58 students who attended six or more sessions, 41 improved by at least one letter grade in the class for which they sought help.
The pilot ran twice a week for one semester.
options.whyWrong: This describes the program but does not show an academic outcome.

explanation.whyCorrect: The grade-change result directly measures an academic outcome among regular participants.
explanation.quickTip: Match the evidence to the exact claim; relevant evidence must address the same question the claim raises.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly supports the claim that the program addresses barriers to tutoring access?

options.text: Tutors said the large room became noisy when more than twenty students arrived.
options.whyWrong: Room noise concerns program operation, not whether the service reaches families facing access barriers.

options.text: Sixty-three percent of participating students came from households that had identified cost or transportation as a barrier.
The director recommends using two smaller rooms next year.
options.whyWrong: A proposed change does not show who the program reached during the pilot.

options.text: Students may also have received classroom help during the semester.
options.whyWrong: This qualifies the grade evidence but does not address access.

explanation.whyCorrect: This statistic connects actual participants to the exact barriers the program was intended to reduce.
explanation.quickTip: Look for evidence that measures the population or outcome named in the claim.

questions.prompt: A student says, “The center is convenient for many families.” Which detail best supports that statement?

options.text: The center is within walking distance of two apartment complexes and is served by an evening bus route.
The tutoring program met twice a week for one semester.
options.whyWrong: Frequency does not show whether the location is convenient.

options.text: Forty-one regular participants improved by at least one letter grade.
options.whyWrong: This concerns academic outcomes, not location convenience.

options.text: Some students stopped attending after sports seasons began.
options.whyWrong: This describes scheduling pressure, not geographic or transportation convenience.

explanation.whyCorrect: Walking access and an evening bus are concrete details that directly support a claim about convenience.
explanation.quickTip: When a claim uses a broad word such as convenient, find the concrete detail that gives that word evidence.

questions.prompt: Which detail would be LEAST useful as evidence for deciding whether the program should continue?

options.text: Attendance patterns across the semester.
options.whyWrong: Attendance helps show whether students actually use the service.

options.text: Changes in course performance among regular participants.
options.whyWrong: Academic outcomes bear directly on whether tutoring may be useful.

options.text: The color of the walls in the community center lobby.
The percentage of participants who faced cost or transportation barriers.
options.whyWrong: This helps evaluate whether the program reaches students with access needs.

explanation.whyCorrect: Lobby color has no meaningful connection to the program's academic value, usage, or access goals.
explanation.quickTip: Relevant evidence must help answer the decision question; details can be true and still be useless evidence.

questions.prompt: Raman argues for a longer trial rather than claiming the program is already proven. Which detail best explains that caution?

options.text: The center is near two apartment complexes.
options.whyWrong: Location does not explain why the academic results should be interpreted cautiously.

options.text: The family survey included 212 households.
options.whyWrong: The survey size is context for access evidence, not the main reason for caution about causation.

options.text: The tutors want to use two rooms next year.
options.whyWrong: The room proposal addresses noise rather than whether tutoring caused grade changes.

options.text: Students who improved may also have studied more or received other help, so the records do not isolate tutoring as the cause.

explanation.whyCorrect: This detail identifies alternative explanations for the improvement and therefore limits what the pilot evidence can prove.
explanation.quickTip: Evidence can support continuing a test without proving a cause; look for details that limit certainty.

questions.prompt: Which pair of details gives evidence for TWO different reasons to continue the pilot?

options.text: Forty-one regular participants improved at least one letter grade; 63 percent of participants came from households reporting cost or transportation barriers.
The room became noisy; sports seasons affected attendance.
options.whyWrong: Both details describe problems rather than different benefits of continuation.

options.text: The center has an evening bus route; the director wants reservations next year.
options.whyWrong: The bus route relates to access, but a proposed reservation system does not establish a second benefit.

options.text: The pilot ran for a semester; the grant is expiring.
options.whyWrong: These facts explain timing but do not provide evidence of academic value or access.

explanation.whyCorrect: One detail supports possible academic benefit and the other supports improved access, giving two distinct evidence lines.
explanation.quickTip: When asked for multiple reasons, make sure each detail supports a different part of the argument.

questions.prompt: Which statement is evidence rather than a claim or recommendation?

options.text: The center should keep tutoring for another year.
options.whyWrong: This is the main recommendation to be supported.

options.text: A longer trial would be the fairest way to judge the program.
options.whyWrong: This is an evaluative claim, not an observed result.

options.text: Forty-one of 58 students who attended six or more sessions improved by at least one letter grade.
The program may be a useful long-term solution for the neighborhood.
options.whyWrong: This is an interpretation of the pilot, not the underlying evidence.

explanation.whyCorrect: This is a specific observed result that can be used to support or challenge a claim.
explanation.quickTip: Evidence is the information you can point to; a claim is what someone wants you to believe about that information.

questions.prompt: Which additional evidence would MOST strengthen the academic case for continuing the program?

options.text: A list of the snacks served during tutoring sessions.
options.whyWrong: Snacks do not measure academic outcomes or isolate the program's effect.

options.text: A comparison of similar students who used tutoring regularly with students who did not, while tracking their course performance over the same period.
A statement from the director saying she believes tutoring works.
options.whyWrong: The director's belief adds little beyond the claim already being evaluated.

options.text: A photograph showing that the tutoring room was often full.
options.whyWrong: A full room can show use, but not whether tutoring improved course performance.

explanation.whyCorrect: A comparison group observed over the same period would make it easier to judge whether improvement is associated with tutoring rather than other changes.
explanation.quickTip: The strongest added evidence addresses the biggest uncertainty in the existing evidence.
explanation.evidenceRef: The records do not prove tutoring caused every improvement.

curriculum.learningObjective: Locate evidence that directly supports a specific claim and distinguish it from background, limitations, and recommendations.
